newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine court ruling may cheer stocks - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Philippine court ruling may cheer stocks - analyst.

text.p: The Philippine Supreme Court's decision to deny President Fidel Ramos a second term of office may bring cheer to the country's lacklustre equities market, analysts said on Tuesday.
"The government has realised that it cannot forever move its goal posts," said Saturnino Mejia, research head at Guoco Securities.
"This Supreme Court decision could create some positive sentiment, a technical rally. It would probably put some sense of a clearer picture of the political exercise in 1998."
The constitution provides the president with a single term of six years and Ramos's term ends in June 1998.

The vote among the Supreme Court members was a tie, which meant its previous decision disallowing a move by a citizens' group to initiate a referendum on lifting the term limits of the president was maintained.
"The market's reaction should be positive. At this point, the decision will stabilise the movement of the market," said Jidgette Valenzuela, research manager at Lippo Securities.

"My feeling is that foreign investors will see that the law has been upheld and that everyone is not wishy-washy here. But it would not impact much on the market," said Jose Ricardo Garcia, executive vice-president at Diversified Securities.
Some analysts maintained the market would need more compelling news such as improved second quarter corporate earnings to spur heavy buying.

The Philippine stock market has been trading in a tight band after a moderate recovery from a battering brought about by fears of a glut in the property sector and a financial crisis similar to that suffered by Thailand.
The Makati Business Club (MBC), a group of top business executives, welcomed the court decision.
"We are happy they have sustained the decision... I think we would have had a more negative situation if the Supreme Court had changed its ruling," said Guillermo Luz, MBC's executive director.
Analysts expect the decision will result in investors keeping a tight watch on domestic politics.

"We always thought that President Ramos would not run. But the more important thing is that the Supreme Court decision will open up Congress to new blood," said Joey Cuyegkeng, reaearch head at ING Barings.
"Investors will be watching closely in the next few months as critical political forces realign themselves," he said.
Cilette Liboro, research head at Orion-Squire Capital, said: "The market will be more focused with one question on their minds, and that's who will win in the 1998 elections."
